A user says Twilio-issued VoIP numbers work well for registering Signal when they don't want to use their cellular carrier number, making SIM-swapping harder because attackers don't know their real number.

A user questions what role the compromised Twilio employee had, and why employee credentials allowed access to plain-text auth codes sent to end users. They argue that permission should be extremely limited.
Another commenter sees the 1,900 affected users as an impressively small upper bound, implying Signal and Twilio caught the breach very quickly. They call the response swift.

On Twilio's admission that Authy data leaked via an unauthenticated endpoint: "This is truly unacceptable for an authentication product. An authentication product that doesn't implement authentication correctly in their own APIs?"

A user who just migrated off Authy says they never liked it and that Twilio makes exporting data extremely difficult. The third-party export tool they used turned out to rely on the same unauthenticated endpoint used in the breach.

A user reports finding an information-exposure bug in Authy's registration endpoint. Given a phone number, it returned the user's other numbers, devices, timestamps and email addresses. They say Twilio took two years to fix it.
A user asks what people use instead of Twilio, complaining that Twilio's 2FA verifications take too long.
A user calls Authy "basically unsupported" and says they moved their accounts to 1Password when Twilio announced end of life for the macOS app.
A user who used SendGrid and Twilio years ago says the pair "basically solved the email and SMS dev-ops problem for more product focused engineers like myself."
A developer says they reach for Twilio/SendGrid whenever a client asks for SMS and transactional email: "Their UX is miles better than any AWS offering."

A user complains that TwiML bins, the easiest way to use Twilio without external hosting, have no email verb or email functionality, not even in Twilio Functions. Simply cc'ing an incoming SMS to email requires hosting your own code or a SendGrid account.

A user dislikes Twilio's "open source" video apps, calling them demo code for a paid proprietary backend. They add that Twilio has a very easy-to-use API, and if usage cost matters less than development time, it's an easy choice.

A commenter says Twilio "make very complicated things very simple and offer a lot of value." However, the open-source client release feels like OSS-washing meant to pull users into Twilio's ecosystem.

A former Twilio employee building a virtual office (all audio muted, grid layout, persistent rooms) says Twilio Video is programmable rather than merely configurable like Jitsi or Zoom, enabling requirements those tools couldn't meet.

A hobbyist used Twilio for years to send calendar alarms by SMS and found it easy and cheap. Twilio then demanded business registration paperwork that made no sense for a hobbyist, so they turned SMS off. They still use Twilio for voicemail-to-webhook with transcription.

A former CTO of a consumer texting company says Twilio does a good job monitoring messages. Its automated system caught spammers abusing their platform and asked them for proof of permission to message those numbers.

A user with about a dozen numbers for small automations says Twilio has been very heavy-handed over the past 6 months about 10DLC registration. The requirements have expanded from high-volume senders to their one-message-a-day accounts.

A user calls Twilio paternalistic and says getting SMS numbers in Germany through it is the worst. Twilio restricts service for anyone without a big company, so they ended up buying a Raspberry Pi and SIM for a client instead.
A user who traced spam calls and texts to originating carriers found Twilio in the top 5 sources. As a share of its total traffic, though, Twilio was nowhere near Commio/Teli or Telnyx.
Another user doesn't get the hate for Twilio, saying they've found Twilio generally responsive when issues are brought up.
